A DAW can show your music two ways. The **Arrangement** is a timeline: bar 1 on the left, the end of the song on the right, every clip
in its place. The **Session** is a grid: each column is a track, each row is a **scene**, and each box is a **clip** that *loops*
until you launch something else. Ableton Live calls these Session View and Arrangement View; Logic Pro's version of the grid is **Live Loops**.

Producers move between the two all the time. Start with a loop that sounds good, copy it into the grid, make a few variations,
perform them in any order, and record that performance as the arrangement. This lesson walks that path once, with a song whose
harmony is simple enough to see: **"The Lion Sleeps Tonight"**.

## The chord roots come first

The song's chords, in the version people usually learn, are **I – IV – I – V**. In the key of F that is **F, B♭, F, C**: one chord a bar.
(That is the progression as commonly taught; I have not checked it against the recording, so listen and decide. The tempo, the parts and
the scenes below are this site's own, not a transcription.)

The **root** of a chord is the note it is named for, and the bass player plays it. That makes the bass the easiest place to *see* the
harmony: in a four-bar loop, the lowest note of each bar spells the chords. Everything else (the organ's triads, the electric piano's
chant figure) is built on those four notes. Keep that in mind: when the roots change, everyone else has to follow.

## 1. Find the loop (Arrangement)

Here is one four-bar loop in the Arrangement: drums, bass, organ pad, and an empty Chant track. The ruler's bracket is already round bars 1–4.

1. Press **▶ Play**. The loop repeats because **⟲ Loop** is on.
2. Click the Bass clip and read the piano roll's lowest notes: **F, B♭, F, C**, one a bar. Those are the roots.
3. Mute the bass (**M**) and listen: the organ still plays the chords, but the floor has gone.

<div class="mdaw" data-id="daw-session-1" data-preset="lionloop" data-show="session transport tracks editor mixer"></div>

## 2. Copy the loop into the Session

Press **Loop → scene**. Everything inside the loop bracket (bars 1–4) is copied into a new **scene**: a looping clip for each track that played.
Then press **Session** to change views. (The Arrangement is untouched; this made copies.)

The scene's row shows its **Roots**, read from the bass: F, B♭, F, C, each with its place in the key (I, IV, I, V).

This is the step that generalizes. In Ableton you drag clips or whole scenes between the views; in Logic you drag a region into a Live
Loops cell or a cell into the Tracks area. The idea is the same: **a loop is a region plus the promise that it repeats**.

## 3. Launch scenes

This grid already has four scenes made from the same roots. Try them in order, then any way you like.

<div class="mdaw" data-id="daw-session-2" data-preset="lion" data-show="session transport tracks editor mixer"></div>

1. Press the **▶ beside Intro**. Nothing happens until the next **bar line**, then the whole row starts: this wait is **launch quantization**.
   It is why clips launched at different moments still land together. Set **Launch** to *on the next beat* and try it: it still works, but
   things can arrive off the bar.
2. Launch **Groove**, then **Chant**. Each track now plays its clip from the new scene. A track plays one clip at a time, so launching a
   clip *replaces* what that track was playing.
3. Launch just the **Bass** clip in Intro while Chant plays: the whole-note bass takes over and everything else carries on. Scenes are
   whole pictures; single clips are how you mix and match.
4. Launch **Break**: two bars of just the V chord with no drums. In this DAW an **empty slot stops its track** when its scene launches,
   so Drums and Chant go quiet. (Check what your own DAW does with empty slots; it differs between programs.)
5. **■ Stop all** stops everything at the next bar line; press it again to stop at once.

### Change the roots, change the song

Click a **root** in the Groove row (say the second F, bar 3). It goes to **B♭**, then **C**, then back to **F**: I, IV, V. The bass
note in that bar moves, and so do the organ's chord and the chant, because they sit on the same root. Make bar 3 a V and the progression
is I – IV – V – V. Does it still sound like the same song? Which change makes it sound most different? Which sounds finished?

The roots only cycle through I, IV and V. That is on purpose: those three chords are all **major** in a major key, so moving a major triad
up or down by the same interval gives the right chord. A ii or a vi is minor and would need its notes changed, not just moved.

### Change the key

Use **Key** to move the song to suit a singer: pick **G** and every pitched note moves up two semitones. The roots update (G, C, G, D), the
numbers underneath (I, IV, I, V) stay the same, and the drums don't change at all. The *numbers* describe the music; the *letters* describe where
you put it.

## 4. Record the performance into the Arrangement

1. Press **● Record to Arrangement**. It waits for the next bar line, then starts logging.
2. Launch scenes and clips in an order you like, say Intro, Groove, Chant, Groove, Chant, Break, Chant.
3. Press the record button again (or **Stop all**). It ends at the next bar line.
4. The view switches to the **Arrangement**: your performance is there as ordinary clips, each loop written out as many times as it played and
   cut at the bar lines. Press **▶ Play** to hear it as a song, edit the clips, or **Undo** to go back.

That is the whole path: *loop → scene → variations → performance → arrangement.* Only the performance part is improvised; everything else is
decisions about which notes repeat and who plays when.

## Things to try

- Make a new scene by copying **Chant** (**⎘**) and changing its roots to something other than I – IV – I – V. Record a performance in which
  the new scene is the "bridge".
- Double-click an empty slot (say Chant in Intro) to make a clip, then write a part in the piano roll that fits the roots.
- Change the **Tempo**, play a scene, and listen to whether the groove still feels right.
- In the first DAW above, press **Loop → scene** twice with different loop brackets (drag along the ruler) to turn bars 1–2 and 3–4
  into separate scenes.

## In other DAWs

<div class="daw-map">

| | Ableton Live | Logic Pro |
|---|---|---|
| The grid is | **Session View** | **Live Loops** |
| A box in the grid | Clip, with a launch (▶) button | Cell |
| A scene is | A row (its launch button is in the Main track column) | A column |
| Play the grid | Launch clips or scenes; one clip per track plays | Play cells or scenes; one cell per track plays |
| Grid → timeline | Record the Session into the Arrangement (the Arrangement Record button) | Enable Performance Recording, then Record; or drag cells and scenes to the Tracks area |
| Back to the grid | **Back to Arrangement** returns tracks to the timeline after a clip is launched | Playback comes from the grid *or* the Tracks area on each track |

</div>

BandLab has loops and regions but, as far as I checked, no clip launcher; I have not verified that. The small DAW here is a model of the
idea, not a copy of either program.
